newsitem.title: USA: Chinese in North Ameria watch Hong Kong handover.
newsitem.headline: Chinese in North Ameria watch Hong Kong handover.

text.p: Chinese in major North American cities watched and celebrated on Monday as China took control of Hong Kong from Britain, but some protested and said they feared for human rights.
Thousands gathered in the Chinatown section of New York City, gleefully waving flags and cheering the floats in a colourful parade.
"This is a glorious day for us, especially since it's a peaceful day," said parade organiser Yi Lum. "We feel very proud that Hong Kong is being returned to China. We see a very bright future."

Folk singers adorned in silk and flowers sang traditional songs, dancing dragon puppets entertained little children and community leaders drew loud cheers from the crowds with chants of "Long Live China."
One float depicted two hands shaking and proclaimed "Everlasting peace with America."
"We're here to show our love for our country," said teenager Andy Sit, who marched in the parade. "Hong Kong is Chinese. It should be part of China."
"Hong Kong will still be free economically to be capitalist," a beaming Jean Zhu said. "It will be an opportunity to show the government the benefits and problems of capitalism."

But outside the Chinese Embassy, dissident Lian Shengde, a leader of the 1989 Tiananmen Square protest who was granted political asylum in the United States last year, spoke of his concern for Hong Kong.

"This should not be a day of celebration," he said. "July 1 is a very sad day. This is not about China getting back land they once had. It's about totalitarianism spreading into a free, democratic and prosperous region."
In Washington, President Bill Clinton said he expected China would be obliged to allow some "dissent" in the region under its 1984 agreement with Britain.

"The agreement says that there will be one China and two systems," he said. "And it's hard to have a system with free elections and freedom of speech and open press without dissent. I can't imagine how you could have it any other way."

Across the continent in Vancouver, Canada, which has seen a dramatic influx of immigrants from Hong Kong in recent years, celebrations included an early morning party at a classical garden in the city's Chinatown.
Demonstrators scheduled pro-democracy protests outside Chinese diplomatic posts in Vancouver, Toronto and Ottawa.

"With the largest Hong Kong immigrant population in the world, the Chinese communities in Canada are visibly concerned about the loss of civil liberties after the handover," said Henry Chau, head of the Vancouver Society in Support of Democratic Movement.
More than 600,000 people of Chinese descent live in Canada, mostly in Toronto and Vancouver. About two-thirds of them are from Hong Kong.
"We wholeheartedly support the return of Hong Kong to China, but we don't think everything is going to be smooth sailing," Chau said.
"We have to be vigilant to guard against further erosion of human rights and fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong."

At the United Nations, U.N. employees crowded around television sets as the red flag of China was hoisted over Hong Kong, with Chinese staff clapping loudly at midnight Hong Kong time -- precisely noon in New York.
